explanations.explanation: That's it. The very next verse says she was pregnant and crying out in the pain and agony of giving birth. She's dressed in the sun and the moon is at her feet, and the real action is still what's happening with her child. I've seen that kind of glow-up in my bakery, and it never changes the fact that there's work to do.

explanations.answer: She's leading an army of angels
explanations.explanation: No army with her, friend. The text only tells us she was pregnant and crying out in the pain and agony of giving birth. Angels do show up later in the chapter, when Michael and his angels fight in heaven (Revelation 12:7), but that's a separate scene. Here she's the one who needs help, not the one with a battalion.

She isn't falling anywhere. She appears as a great sign in heaven, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head. The falling comes in verse 4, and that's stars being swept from the sky, not her. I'd be dizzy too if I had to keep track of who's dropping, so let's keep her feet firmly on that moon.

Yes, a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven royal crowns on his heads. The woman is called a sign, and so is he, and that's a lot of sign for one sky. Notice he's another sign appearing in heaven, right alongside her. You don't need a pastry degree to tell this guy is trouble.

That's a real image in Revelation, but it's from a different scene. John saw a pale horse back in Revelation 6:8. In this vision the second sign is a huge red dragon, and he didn't come in on a horse. Different vision, different animal, and this one has way more heads.

Golden lampstands are in Revelation too, just earlier. John saw seven golden lampstands in Revelation 1:12. What shows up in heaven right after the woman is a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven royal crowns. I'd take a nice lampstand over that, but we don't get to pick the signs.

Close, but that's too big. The text says his tail swept a third of the stars from the sky, hurling them to the earth. A third is a huge sweep, but the sky still has stars left. Every last star would be a whole different verse.

Right, it's not every last star. Verse 4 says his tail swept a third of the stars from the sky, hurling them to the earth. That's one swish of a tail and a third of the stars are gone. Even so, the text keeps the number exactly where it is, so we do too.

explanations.answer: To devour her child as soon as it's born
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, ready to devour her child as soon as she gave birth. He wasn't there for the view. I think the whole scene gets very quiet right here, and it's a hard one to sit with.

explanations.answer: To snatch the crown off her head
explanations.explanation: The crown of twelve stars is on her head, but the dragon isn't there for it. The text says he stood ready to devour her child as soon as she gave birth. It's the child he's after, and that's a lot heavier than jewelry.

explanations.answer: To steal the moon from under her feet
explanations.explanation: The moon is under her feet, but the dragon has no interest in it. Verse 4 says he stood before the woman who was about to give birth, ready to devour her child as soon as she gave birth. His target is the child. The sky decorations are not on his list.

It looks that way with the dragon standing right there, but the text says otherwise. Verse 5 says her child was caught up to God and to His throne. So the dragon never gets his hands on him. Whatever he planned, the child is taken up before it happens.

Right. The dragon is ready and waiting, but verse 5 says her child was caught up to God and to His throne. He gets nowhere near him. When the dragon's plan hits a wall like that, I'd love to have seen the look on all seven faces.

Yes, the wilderness. The woman fled there, to a place God had prepared for her. The place was ready before she got there. That's the kind of detail a baker appreciates, because I like it when the oven is already warm.

The text doesn't send her to a temple. It says the woman fled into the wilderness, where God had prepared a place for her. A wilderness is a wide, empty kind of place, nothing like a building. It's still a place God prepared, and that's the part that matters.

No city here. Verse 6 says the woman fled into the wilderness, where God had prepared a place for her to be nourished. Wilderness means open country, not streets and rooftops. I know a city has a bakery on every corner, but that's not where she was headed.

That's what it says. Verse 8 says the dragon was not strong enough, and no longer was any place found in heaven for him and his angels. Michael and his angels fought, the dragon and his angels fought back, and the dragon still came up short. A guy with seven heads and he still can't win.

It's the other way around. The text says the dragon was not strong enough, and no longer was any place found in heaven for him and his angels. They fought back, but it didn't get them anywhere. The war ends with him on the losing side.

explanations.answer: The ancient serpent called the devil
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Verse 9 says the great dragon is that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. John, who wrote this book, doesn't leave us guessing. The dragon is named plainly, and that settles it.

Nebuchadnezzar was a real king of Babylon who took Jerusalem's people into exile (Daniel 1:1). But he isn't who the dragon is. Verse 9 says the great dragon is that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan. This dragon isn't an earthly king, no matter how many crowns he's wearing.

Goliath was a giant from Gath, the Philistine champion David faced (1 Samuel 17:4). But the dragon isn't him. John tells us the great dragon is that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. Big and loud isn't a match, because this one is a whole other story.

explanations.answer: The accuser of our brothers is thrown down
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the voice gives. It says, “For the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down—he who accuses them day and night before our God.” His being hurled out of heaven is why the voice announces it now. When the accuser is out, the announcement can come.

explanations.answer: The woman has come back from the wilderness
explanations.explanation: The woman isn't back yet. Verse 14 has her flying to her place in the wilderness, where she was nourished. The voice gives a different reason: the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down. Her trip home isn't part of the announcement.

explanations.answer: The dragon has surrendered his crowns
explanations.explanation: He doesn't hand over anything. The text says he was hurled down, and then the voice says the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down. That's being thrown, not giving up. I've never met a seven-headed fellow who surrenders politely.

explanations.answer: By the blood of the Lamb and their testimony
explanations.explanation: Exactly. The voice says, “They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony.” The Lamb is Jesus, whom John the Baptist called “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). The victory rests on Him and on what they say about Him.

explanations.answer: By the strength of their hands and their courage
explanations.explanation: Not by their own muscle. The voice says they conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. The strength is not theirs. I've lifted a lot of cookie boxes and none of them ever beat a dragon.

explanations.answer: By the wisdom of the elders and their prayers
explanations.explanation: The voice doesn't name that. It says, “They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony.” Prayer and wise people are good things, but they're not what this verse names. The text gives the Lamb and their testimony.

Rejoice is the word. The voice says, “Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them!” The accuser has been thrown down, so the heavens get to celebrate. I'd be tossing sprinkles right now if my planet had a heaven nearby.

No trembling is called for in heaven. The voice says, “Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them!” The accuser is already thrown down. The trouble in this verse is aimed at the earth and the sea, not the heavens.

Mourning isn't what the heavens are told to do. The voice says, “Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them!” The woe comes next, but it's for the earth and the sea. Heaven gets the celebration.

That's right. The voice says, “But woe to the earth and the sea; with great fury the devil has come down to you, knowing he has only a short time.” He's been thrown down, and now he's here. It's a serious line, so I'd read it slowly.

The text says it plainly. The voice says, “But woe to the earth and the sea; with great fury the devil has come down to you, knowing he has only a short time.” So he has come down, and he's furious. That's the reason for the woe on the earth and the sea.

Yes. Verse 13 says that when the dragon saw he had been thrown to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. He lost the war in heaven and went right after her. Some folks lose and walk it off. He doesn't.

It's true, actually. Verse 13 says when the dragon saw that he had been thrown to the earth, he pursued the woman who had given birth to the male child. He doesn't stay down and he doesn't give up. He goes straight after her.

explanations.answer: She's given two wings of a great eagle
explanations.explanation: Yes, two wings of a great eagle. Verse 14 says she was given them to fly from the presence of the serpent to her place in the wilderness. Notice she's given the wings. She didn't earn them or build them.

explanations.answer: She hides in a cave beside the sea
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have a cave. It says the woman was given two wings of a great eagle to fly from the presence of the serpent to her place in the wilderness. She flies, she doesn't hide. And the sea only comes up later, at the end of the chapter, where the dragon stands on the shore.

explanations.answer: An angel carries her off on a cloud
explanations.explanation: No angel and no cloud in this verse. The woman was given two wings of a great eagle to fly from the presence of the serpent to her place in the wilderness. The wings are the way out. Angels are busy elsewhere in this chapter, with Michael in verse 7.

explanations.answer: The earth opens up and swallows it
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Verse 16 says the earth helped the woman and opened its mouth to swallow up the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. The ground itself steps in on her side. I love it when the floor shows up to help.

Michael is the angel who fought the dragon in heaven in verse 7, but he isn't in this scene. Verse 16 says the earth helped the woman and opened its mouth to swallow up the river. So the help comes from the earth, not from an angel's sword.

explanations.answer: The sun dries it all up
explanations.explanation: The sun was her clothing back in verse 1, but it doesn't dry anything here. Verse 16 says the earth helped the woman and opened its mouth to swallow up the river that the dragon had poured from his mouth. The ground does the job, and that's a cleanup I'd happily hire.

That can't happen, because he was already thrown out. Verse 8 says no longer was any place found in heaven for him and his angels. After he's enraged, verse 17 says he went to make war with the rest of her children. He stays on the earth.

Right. Verse 17 says the dragon was enraged at the woman and went to make war with the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus. He doesn't go back to heaven, since there's no place left for him there (Revelation 12:8). His anger takes him toward them.
